questions.prompt: Put this sentence into the negative, keeping the same tense: "They have made a new offer."

options.text: They didn't make a new offer.
They haven't made a new offer already.
They haven't made a new offer.
They haven't make a new offer.

questions.explanation: The negative of the present perfect keeps the auxiliary and adds not, leaving the participle alone: "They haven't made a new offer." "They didn't make a new offer." is well formed, but it moves the sentence to the simple past, which the instruction forbids. "They haven't make a new offer." replaces the participle with the base form. "They haven't made a new offer already." uses already in a negative, where English puts yet at the end: They haven't made a new offer yet.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The language centre ___ any new students in 2021."
questions.explanation: "in 2021" names a finished past time, so the sentence needs the simple past negative, which is didn't followed by the base verb: "didn't accept". "didn't accepted" keeps a past ending after did, which already carries the past on its own. "doesn't accept" is a present form, and "hasn't accepted" places a present perfect beside a stated time, which that tense never accepts.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The two brothers ___ the old mill three years ago, and today it is a small museum."
questions.explanation: "three years ago" points at a finished moment, so the sentence takes the simple past, and repair is a regular verb: "repaired". The result visible today is tempting, but "have repaired" and "has repaired" place a present perfect beside a stated time, which that tense refuses — and has would not even agree with the two brothers. "repair" is a present form and leaves the sentence with no past at all.

2017 is a starting point, not a length of time, so the sentence takes since; and a situation that runs from 2017 to today takes the present perfect, with a singular subject: "has owned ... since". "has owned ... for" would need a duration such as ten years. "owned ... since" leaves a simple past hanging on a starting point that reaches the present. "have owned ... since" gives Rami the plural auxiliary.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Since April, the two studios ___ four projects together."
questions.explanation: Since April gives a starting point, so the sentence calls for the present perfect, and the participle of begin is begun: "have begun". "have began" puts the simple past after have, which the tense never allows. "began" on its own cannot stand with since. "has already begun" hands a singular auxiliary to a plural subject, the two studios.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The two sisters ___ the second-hand bookshop in 2015 and they ___ it themselves since then."
questions.explanation: The two halves of the sentence do not share one tense: in 2015 is a stated date, so the first verb is a simple past, while since then reaches today, so the second is a present perfect — "restored ... have managed". "restored ... managed" leaves a simple past hanging on since then. "have restored ... managed" swaps the two tenses. "have restored ... have managed" puts a present perfect right next to the date 2015.
